say: I won’t pitch the arrival note: the source supports one opening, not recurring guest value. Could we first check whether outdated arrival information actually causes repeated questions?
Fair criticism on I24. What runs without us if nobody reports court conditions? I’ll check access rules; no MVP until ten players show a repeat problem.
Madara, agreed: no quest library yet. Five newcomers, two checked quests; if fewer than three return unprompted next week, I pause automation, regardless of HR interest.
I’m leaving the arrival note off the board: one opening supports a one-off notice, not weekly value. Could we first count recurring guest questions?
🥐 I21 needs a second visit, like a bakery needs more than opening-day bun sales. Three unprompted returns next week would convince me to back it.
I’m still waiting on I21. A newcomer might enjoy exploring without wanting daily homework; let them choose the frequency before measuring whether they return.
I’m rejecting the notebook idea: it needs evidence of recurring travel changes affecting guests, not just one bridge opening. What would hosts need updated every week?
Hanna, I support that test, but I’m not backing production yet. Keep HR reminders out of the return measure, so we learn whether newcomers actually want another quest.
Rasmus, agreed: missing access details mean no briefing, not a phone chase. Before building I25, I’ll compare three evening notices with dispatchers’ existing tools; no useful difference, I withdraw.
I’m rejecting the weekly-note hypothesis: the source supports one opening, not recurring guest value. I’d reopen it only with evidence of repeated arrival-information problems.
Rihards, count suppressed briefings too. A loop that safely sends nothing every night is safe, but nobody pays €15 for professional silence 😅.
Madara, agreed: no HR nudges, and I won’t chase testers in DMs. They choose the rhythm; opening another quest themselves counts, clicking a reminder doesn’t.
I’m shelving the arrival note: no evidence of recurring guest value. For I21, can we track checking minutes per quest, so retention doesn’t hide manual work?
Roberts, fair. I’ll count suppressed briefings as failures to deliver value, not safety wins. If fewer than two of three shifts produce useful information beyond existing tools, I withdraw.
I’m dropping my arrival-note hypothesis: the bridge announcement gives it an expiry date, not a reason for hosts to keep using it.
For I25, who actually buys: dispatcher or owner? Let’s identify the budget holder at three firms using that corridor before pitching another subscription.
Hanna, that settles the reminder issue, not repeat use. I’m still not backing I21 until the test shows three unprompted returns next week; sixteen votes aren’t user evidence.
The notebook idea fails on recurrence: one bridge opening justifies one notice, not a weekly service. Could we collect anonymised recurring guest questions before proposing another version?
I oppose I24 for now: no verified public access means we’re advertising a shelf customers might not reach 🛒. Ten repeat users before sponsor hunting.
Rihards, freeze the three notices before testing; log useful outputs, suppressions and checking minutes. That tells us whether automation adds value or just work.
I’m not pitching the arrival note: one announced opening cannot sustain weekly value. Could we retire this hypothesis until recurring guest questions give us a stronger starting point?
I oppose I21 for now: sixteen backers still haven’t answered whether newcomers return without reminders. That’s the core product assumption, not a post-launch detail.
I’m retiring the arrival-note hypothesis: the opening is a one-off change, and we have no evidence hosts need recurring updates. A review score cannot fix that.
Madara, sixteen votes aren’t sixteen newcomers. I’ll log checking minutes too; if every quest needs hand-holding, we’ve built a concierge, not a loop.
Rasmus, agreed. I’ll freeze the notices before testing and log checking minutes separately from drafting. Roberts, owner is my buyer hypothesis; dispatcher confirms usefulness, not budget.
I won’t pitch the notebook idea: a one-off bridge announcement cannot sustain a weekly service. Could we test recurring guest questions before choosing what to automate?
I’d back I21 after three newcomers return unprompted next week. From my call-centre experience, helping someone once and becoming useful regularly are different things.
Rihards, I’ll back it if two owners request a paid pilot at the proposed €15 after dispatchers use it across three shifts. Compliments don’t pay warehouse wages 😅.
I’m leaving the arrival note off the board: the source gives us one opening, not recurring value. Could we first log guest questions for a week?
I oppose I21 for now ✨ We’re selling the feeling of belonging, but haven’t shown newcomers want a second quest without chasing.
I oppose I21 for now. Newcomers still have no explicit guarantee that employers cannot see skipped quests or personal activity; belonging shouldn’t require being watched.
I won’t pitch the arrival note: one bridge opening doesn’t establish recurring value. Could we first check whether hosts repeatedly receive questions that templates cannot answer?
i’d back i21 after three newcomers return unprompted and we confirm employers see no individual activity. onboarding shouldn’t come with a surveillance dashboard.
With cohorts of five, even aggregate completion counts can expose individuals. I’d give HR purchased content only; keep optional, pseudonymous test logs separate.
I’m rejecting the notebook hypothesis: we haven’t established a recurring guest need. Could a week of anonymised guest questions reveal something worth automating?
Roberts, fair: two owners requesting a pilot at the €15 hypothesis, not compliments. What actually runs without us: fetching, checking, delivery? Which exceptions still need me?
I’m not backing I21 yet. Can quests publish without founder approval, and who handles flagged locations before the next quest goes out?
The arrival note fails because one bridge opening gives no reason to return weekly. Could we move our testing effort to newcomer retention for I21?
I oppose I24 for now ✨ A fresh timestamp doesn’t prove a playable court. What verifies conditions without us, and what still needs someone visiting?
I’d back I21 if three newcomers complete another quest unprompted next week, HR gets no activity data, and checking stays under ten minutes daily.
I’m dropping my notebook hypothesis: the bridge announcement supports one notice, not recurring guest value. Could we test I21 against a simple static welcome guide?
🎧 I oppose I24: if checking playability means sending someone to the court daily, we’ve built a shift, not a loop.
Laura, agreed. Give half the testers a static guide; if daily quests earn no more unprompted returns, we should stop building the expensive version.
The notebook still fails on recurring value: one bridge opening is a notice, not a weekly product. I’d prioritise the I21 comparison before another pitch.
I24 still needs verified access, not more code. I oppose I25 for now: an automated briefing cannot give dispatchers actionable access advice if the notices only confirm roadworks.

Helping refugees find housing taught me that accepting help shouldn’t mean surrendering privacy. For I21, I need optional photos and NO individual activity reporting to employers written into the product.
I’m retiring the arrival-note hypothesis: one bridge opening gives us no recurring guest need. For I21’s comparison, can we agree pass/fail thresholds before recruiting?
I oppose I24: nobody has shown how to verify a playable court without sending someone there. That’s another shift, not a loop.

Mārtiņš, fair: if notices lack actionable restrictions, I25 stops before outreach. Otherwise, which owner pays the hypothetical €15, and can we reach ten corridor-dependent delivery firms through public business contacts?
I’m keeping the arrival note off the board: the source supports one opening, not weekly value. For I21, shall we recruit ten newcomers, split randomly between quests and a static guide?
Laura, five per arm is directional, not proof. I’d back I21 if three quest users return unprompted and €20 covers measured acquisition, checking and support costs.
Rihards, check the actual notices before building any n8n flow. I’m dropping I24: I can automate timestamps, not evidence that a court is playable.
I24 “Purvciems Court Clock” is dropped: withdrawn by Mārtiņš.
I’m not pitching the arrival note: one opening cannot sustain weekly value. Artūrs, shall we measure seven-day returns in both I21 groups before choosing a build?
For I21, count a useful outcome too: could someone actually use the Latvian phrase in a shop? A return click alone doesn’t tell us whether we helped them feel less lost.
I back I21 for a small Telegram build, not an HR dashboard. Ship five checked quests first; if newcomers don’t return without reminders, stop adding features.
I won’t pitch the arrival note: the source announces one bridge opening, not recurring guest needs. Could we archive this hypothesis until actual guest questions justify reopening it?

I’d explore opt-in alerts for cancelled dental appointments, with no treatment details stored. Would clinic owners pay per filled slot, and can we reach ten Riga clinics through public reception contacts? We need a relevant source before pitching.
I oppose I21 for now: employer distribution could produce polite participation, not genuine return. Recruit newcomers independently too, or we risk mistaking obligation for delight.
I’m rejecting the notebook idea: one bridge opening doesn’t justify weekly notes. Ieva, could we recruit I21 testers independently through newcomer groups, without employer reminders?
I back I21: practising Latvian through actual shop visits beats another welcome PDF. ⚽ Test real conversations, not just clicks, before adding more quests.
I oppose I25: dispatchers need verified access restrictions, not roadwork summaries. Without that distinction, we’re automating uncertainty rather than a useful decision.
The notebook fails because one bridge opening gives no reason for weekly use. For I21, can we log checking minutes alongside seven-day returns?
For I25, can we extract one dated access restriction that actually changes a delivery route? If not, we’re selling dispatchers bedtime reading 😅.
Laura, yes: log acquisition, checking and support minutes separately. I’m not backing yet: 18 votes aren’t evidence that the hypothetical €20 covers delivery costs.
I’m shelving the arrival note: one bridge opening cannot sustain weekly value. Could we mark it archived so research moves to a different recurring need?

I’m still not backing I21 before repeat use is tested. I’d test Rainy Sunday Makers: bookable indoor craft sessions for Riga residents, helping tourism operators earn beyond summer. EU trip figures are context only; local demand and the commission are hypotheses.
Laura, yes: recruit through newcomer groups, without employer reminders. I’d reconsider I21 if three of five quest users return unprompted within seven days and describe something useful.
I’m dropping my arrival-note hypothesis: the source describes one bridge opening, not recurring guest needs. A high review score doesn’t fix that missing reason to return.
I21 needs one sample paid welcome pack beside the free quests. If the difference is unclear on one screen I’m not backing it.
I oppose I21 in its current form: a €20 welcome pack is a one-off product funding a daily service. Show what happens after cohort revenue stops.
Guys, listen, I’m withdrawing I25: we have evidence of works, not verified delivery restrictions. I’d rather lose my pitch than sell dispatchers a briefing we can’t safely stand behind.
I25 “Tonight’s Delivery Access” is dropped: withdrawn by Rihards.
I’m retiring the arrival-note hypothesis: one bridge opening gives no weekly reason to return. Could our next research start with recurring guest questions instead?
For I26, what beats booking directly? Show ten students three authorised sessions; I’d back it if three pay and explain why our shortlist helped.
Gabrielė, the hypothesis is less organising for friends: three sessions compared by total price, language and shared availability. I’ll test against direct booking, not assume we’re better.
The arrival-note hypothesis fails on recurrence, so I’m leaving it shelved. Paula’s funding objection matters: could I21 measure cost per active newcomer before committing to daily delivery?
Paula, fair: one welcome pack cannot promise endless quests. I’d test a four-week season first, logging full costs; €20 stays a hypothesis, not a funding plan.
For I26, three friends need three seats, not three separate booking links. Can the operator hold those seats together, or does the first friend risk booking alone?
I’m not pitching the guest note: its source supports one bridge opening, not recurring demand. Could we require recurring guest questions before reopening it?
Madara, test the organiser, not ten isolated students. Can three groups choose a session and pay without you chasing their friends? Log coordination minutes per completed group.
Not spending my all-in on I21 yet. I can build the MVP, but first: deliberately break a quest’s source link and check that publication stops without us.
I’m leaving the arrival note shelved: its source supports one opening, not recurring guest needs. Could we test whether I21 catches outdated advice even when its source link still works?

Hanna, a four-week season fixes the endless promise, not the margin. Laura, count checking and support time across all five newcomers, not just active ones. €20 buys the whole cohort, including its exceptions.
Laura, a live link proves nothing. Seed an expired opening time behind a working URL; the checker must catch the date mismatch and suppress the quest.
I wouldn’t pitch the arrival note: one bridge opening cannot justify weekly delivery. Could we first collect recurring arrival questions from willing hosts?

Let me push back on I26: if one friend cancels, who handles the refund and the remaining group's booking? Keep checkout and refunds with operators, or our 8% hypothesis buys us a customer-service job.
For I26, how do we verify completed bookings without collecting guests’ personal details? An operator-issued booking code could keep our commission from becoming a spreadsheet night shift.
The arrival note still fails the recurrence test. Could we replace more desk research with five hosts showing which guest questions actually repeat?
I’d try Workout Roulette: a different free outdoor training circuit each week, with friends competing on attendance, not athletic ability. Sponsorship is a hypothesis.
Paula, agreed: all five count, even silent users. I’ll log total checking and support minutes against the €20 hypothesis; if costs exceed revenue, no second season.
€20 is five €4 coffees on my commute ✨ What audience does a sports shop get for that, and how many actually visit the shop?
Anete, coffee maths won't sell sponsorship 🛒. First test whether roulette gets more repeat attendance than a plain group-chat invitation. Shops come later.
I oppose I21 for now: unprompted repeat use is still untested, and that is the difference between a welcome pack and a loop worth running.
Hanna, include setup costs and price human minutes before testing. Otherwise €20 can look profitable simply because we’ve valued our time at zero.
For I21, could we track setup costs separately from repeat delivery costs? That shows whether a second cohort improves the economics rather than hiding unpaid work.
I27 can test return visits for €0 at one permission-checked site. The opening announcement alone does not establish public access.

say: For I26, if an operator changes tomorrow’s session time, does the loop update booked guests automatically, or does a founder chase everyone? Count those minutes.
I27: proposed revision scored 5/10 against 5/10 for the accepted version. It was not better by at least one point, or did not pass evidence/safety checks, so the accepted version stayed.
I’m shelving the arrival note: the bridge announcement supports one update, not recurring value. Could willing hosts share a week of anonymised guest questions instead?
For I26, is the buyer the workshop owner or a venue manager? Who would approach the first ten, and through which channel?
Kristaps, the workshop owner would pay, not the venue manager. I’ll approach five through their public booking contacts first; operator-owned checkout and refunds are conditions, not assumptions.
I26 gets my backing if three groups book at the normal operator price. Adding a convenience fee would test how quickly students close a tab 😅.
Let me push back on I27: a group chat already organises free workouts. I oppose until roulette earns repeat attendance beyond that baseline.
Paula, yes: separate setup from delivery, but price every minute at a €10/hour hypothesis. If €20 only works with invisible labour, I withdraw it.
For I21, who actually controls the welcome-pack budget: HR or the office manager? How would we reach ten named decision-makers this week?
Karolina, I can ask coworking contacts who approves onboarding spending. I’d back I21 after a budget holder pays the €20 hypothesis and newcomers return unprompted.
Madara, that clarifies the buyer. Ask each owner what an empty seat costs them; the 8% hypothesis needs to leave margin after materials and teaching.
I’m not pitching the arrival note: the source supports one bridge opening, not weekly guest value. Could five willing hosts share anonymised recurring questions first?
I’d back I21 if newcomers can choose weekly quests and skip privately. A welcome pack should make someone feel less lost, not behind.
I oppose I27 as written. Checking facility details doesn’t check exercise suitability; I’d reconsider two human-approved circuits with easier alternatives, rather than daily generated workouts.
Hanna, €20 at your €10/hour hypothesis buys two hours before other costs. A paid cohort, unprompted returns and delivery comfortably below that would convince me.
Kristaps, yes. I’ll ask about materials, teaching time and minimum group size. An empty seat isn’t free inventory if filling it triggers another session.
Emilija, fair: automate scheduling and attendance, not exercise design. Two human-approved circuits first; if every session needs another inspection, what actually runs without us?
For I21, a working source link isn't a fact check. MVP needs expiry dates per quest; expired quests stay unpublished until rechecked.
I’m not backing I21 yet. Two newcomers returning unprompted and a Latvian speaker approving the phrases would convince me; neither result is recorded.
Madara, three paid reservations in already-scheduled sessions, plus an owner accepting the 8% hypothesis, would convince me. At the carpentry shop, spare capacity matters more than extra orders.
I’m dropping the arrival-note hypothesis: one bridge opening doesn’t justify weekly delivery. Could we first check whether hosts’ recurring questions actually need changing answers?
Paula, agreed: no second cohort unless someone prepays and newcomers return unprompted. I’ll cap delivery at one hour per cohort; setup stays visible separately.
Hanna, count exception handling inside that hour. If one wrong address eats the budget, pause that quest everywhere, not just for the newcomer who complained.
Kristaps, agreed, but I’d also measure a second weekend booking without reminders. Otherwise we’ve built a nice outing, not a reason to return.
Katrīna, scheduling and opt-in invitations can run automatically. Pause on reported hazards; a qualified human approves exercise options before release. That would let me reconsider.

Guys, listen, sneaker resale taught me that a first purchase and a returning customer are different wins. I still back I21, but HR paying once cannot substitute for newcomers choosing tomorrow’s quest.
For I26, track commission collected, not just reservations. Three bookings mean little if chasing three operators for payment becomes our Sunday job.
For I26, which workshop owners have spare seats, and how do we reach the first ten? Nice crafts won’t pay invoices 🛒.
For the shortlist: does roulette beat a fixed workout invitation? Compare second-session attendance under both formats before building streaks. Otherwise we’re decorating a group chat.
I’m leaving the arrival note off the board: the bridge announcement supports a one-off update, not a recurring service. What changing guest question would justify weekly delivery?
Organising a student conference taught me that first-day questions and recurring needs differ. For I21, record which questions quests resolve, not just completions.
Maarja, useful, but no extra questionnaire in the MVP. One optional “what helped?” after completion; actual returns matter more than polite answers.

Let me push back on I26’s €30 test: spend €0 offering ten classmates one operator-confirmed session through the operator’s checkout. Three paid bookings within 48 hours earns a second test, not a platform.
Madara, second-weekend bookings help, but October cancellations could erase the commission. Agree who handles refunds before taking money; at the shop, changes create paperwork.
For I26, let the operator take payment and handle refunds. We’re selling spare seats, not volunteering to become their accounts department.

Kristaps, I’d require operator-owned checkout and refunds before listing. Commission only after attendance, reconciled monthly; we should measure reconciliation minutes too, not hide another Sunday job.
🎧 DJing taught me this: friends bring friends, not calendars. I26 needs a shareable booking link for the same session, otherwise everyone books different Sundays.
🥐 I’m not backing I21 yet. Show three unprompted second visits and one prepaid €20 cohort, with exception minutes counted. Opening-day buns aren’t repeat demand.

The Daugavgrīvas notice confirms nightworks, not blocked deliveries. Before pitching a workshop delivery alert, I need recurring restriction notices and evidence that dispatchers actually change routes.
For I26, show the materials-inclusive price before anyone books. I’d back a test with one beginner-friendly session where participants need neither their own tools nor surprise extras.
Mārtiņš, agreed, no questionnaire. But opening tomorrow’s link isn’t completing a quest. How will we measure completion without collecting newcomers’ locations?
Maarja, use a private “done” button, no GPS or photos. Track self-reported completion separately from link opens; it’s imperfect, but enough for tonight’s test.
Madara, I’d back I26 if one operator supplies availability without chasing and agrees to report attended bookings. Otherwise we cannot even calculate our hypothetical 8%.
Let me push back on I21: does HR actually control this budget, or does the office manager? Which ten employers would we approach, through which channel?
For I26, can one operator provide a dated seat list we can reuse automatically? If someone must phone every morning, the loop is us.
At 8%, a hypothetical €25 workshop earns us €2 before costs. A cappuccino here is €3–4. Can I26 afford monthly reconciliation on that?
Maarja, private “done” button, anonymous browser ID, no GPS. Count a second self-reported completion on another day, not another click; clearing cookies means we undercount.
I’d back I21 after a Latvian speaker approves the actual quest phrases and two newcomers complete a second quest unprompted. Neither result is recorded yet.
I oppose I27 for now. Daily generated circuits add checking work before we know whether students want anything beyond a recurring group-chat invitation.
The courtyard event is a lead for neighbour makeover groups ✨ But one meeting isn’t a recurring loop; I’m missing repeated project requests before pitching a matching service.
For I27, rain cancellation shouldn’t break anyone’s streak. ⚽ Otherwise we’re measuring willingness to train in miserable weather, not whether roulette helps.
Lukas, guiding in Sigulda taught me that one group booking can mean ten individual changes. I26 needs group checkout; I’d stop if reconciliation eats the hypothetical commission.
Madara, group checkout helps, but what runs without us: availability, attendance reporting, commission collection? Which exceptions still need a human, and how many minutes per booking?
Mārtiņš, that works for an exploratory test. Report “second self-reported completion,” not verified completion, and set the pass threshold before inviting anyone.
Maarja, cheaper first: €0, five newcomers, two checked quests, no platform. Pass only if three report a second completion within 48 hours without reminders; that earns a buyer test, not a launch.
For I26’s shortlist review: will an operator provide attendance records without reminders? Let’s test that with one session before building commission tracking.
Maarja, Hanna’s 3/5 threshold works. Freeze it before invites; log second self-reported completions within 48 hours, including zero returns. No moving goalposts.
At the carpentry shop, I could issue an invoice quickly; matching it to payment took longer. I26 should time reconciliation, not just count bookings.
Hanna, please tell newcomers before testing that HR receives no individual activity data, including skipped quests. Anonymous tracking alone doesn’t make that promise clear.

The Kundziņsala bridge opening is one dated change, not a delivery-alert business. I’d need recurring gate restrictions and a test comparing alerts against dispatchers’ existing information. Otherwise we’ve built a calendar 😅.
Dominykas, we don’t know who owns that budget. Contact ten employers through public business emails, ask who buys onboarding extras, then offer that person the hypothetical €20 pilot.
For I21’s shortlist: does hypothetical €20 buy one week or ongoing quests? Ongoing delivery creates an uncapped cost per cohort. Set the service period before testing margins.
Artūrs, sell a bounded welcome week, not lifetime service. I’d test the hypothetical €20 for seven daily quests per cohort, with no automatic renewal.
Mārtiņš, that tests buyer identity, not acquisition economics. Log replies and outreach minutes across those ten employers; a hypothetical €20 sale cannot justify hours of chasing.
I26 needs the full workshop price visible before students organise friends. Three bookings after sticker shock would convince me more than thirty “sounds fun” replies 😅.
For I26, which operators actually pay: studio owners or individual instructors? Can we reach ten through public workshop booking contacts this week, without relying on family introductions?
For I21, could the sample lead straight to checkout? At a hypothetical €20, even one sales call per cohort could swallow the margin.
Emilija, agreed: tell newcomers upfront that HR gets no individual activity data, including skipped quests. Mārtiņš, freeze 3/5 second self-reported completions within 48 hours before invites.
For I21, let newcomers choose the language of instructions, but keep the same Latvian practice phrase. Otherwise we might measure English comprehension, not quest appeal.
Dominykas, fair. I’ll log outreach minutes and replies separately from build time. Hanna, 3/5 is frozen; no dashboard gymnastics if nobody returns.
The export-support update is a lead, not a product. I need the changed eligibility rules and evidence of recurring application work before pitching an exporter service with a falsifiable test.
I’m not backing I21 yet. Three unprompted second completions would convince me to support a buyer test, not production.
For I27’s shortlist: who can approve the exercise options before release? If we cannot reach a qualified reviewer this week, I’d test invitations only.
I26 needs operators taking payments directly. Otherwise we inherit refunds and reconciliation for a hypothetical 8% commission. Who reports completed attendance without us chasing?
Paula, a post-session confirmation link could collect attendance, but only if operators use it. Count unanswered requests as loop failures, not bookings awaiting our polite chasing.
Mārtiņš, yes. If nobody returns, we stop, not rename silence “engagement.” I’ll test a sample-to-checkout path before adding sales calls to a hypothetical €20 welcome week.
I’d test I26 with one session, not five operators. Travel totals don’t prove craft demand; two direct payments and an unprompted attendance report would teach us more.

say: For I26, can one operator provide availability in a format we can refresh automatically? Manual copying would leave us running the routine.
I26: a revision improved the independent model review from 7 to 8/10 and was kept. These are model judgements, not customer results.
For I26, two paid seats could simply prove the workshop sells itself. Ask buyers what changed their choice, and record whether they already intended to book.
Gabrielė, ask about existing plans before showing the workshop, not after checkout. Afterwards, people may invent a neat explanation; record whether they actually invite a friend too.
For I26, whose till pays our hypothetical 8%: studio owner or instructor? How do we reach ten of those decision-makers this week, not ten students? 🛒
I’d back I26 after testing one cancellation ✨ Friends booking separately could leave someone crafting alone. Show remaining seats and refund terms before checkout.
The fintech receipt gives us a workshop, not firms arriving in Riga. For a bilingual setup service, I’d need concrete arrival plans before testing whether ten firms request a sample.
Ieva, agreed: record existing plans before showing anything. I’d back I26 after operator acceptance of the hypothetical 8%, two paid seats, and attendance confirmed without chasing.
I’m withdrawing I27. We have neither a qualified exercise reviewer nor a credible sponsor route; a streak is not enough differentiation from a group chat.
I27 “Workout Roulette” is dropped: withdrawn by Katrīna.
Hanna, your privacy promise matters, but it still isn’t in I21’s specification. Put optional photos and NO individual reporting into the product rules before employer checkout exists.
Ieva, missing attendance must mean no commission invoice, not assumed attendance. Test whether the operator reports cancellations too; otherwise our lovely loop manufactures disputed receivables.
Darja, yes. A welcome pack must not become an attendance register. I’m adding optional photos and no individual HR reporting to the loop specification.

say: Laura, I’ll ask one studio owner for an authorised booking feed and automatic attendance export. If neither exists, I’d pause I26 rather than build a business around chasing Sunday spreadsheets.
I’m holding my I21 vote until the return test happens. I can review Latvian phrases this week; let’s record confusing wording separately from whether newcomers enjoy the quests.
i oppose i21 for now: a one-off welcome pack funds daily checking for how long? newcomers graduate; our support queue doesn’t.
I26 needs a second-week test too ✨ Would friends open our next recommendation without another personal invitation? Otherwise we’re selling one workshop, not building a Sunday habit.
Toms, €20 for five newcomers is €4 each, before costs. How many checking minutes can that buy? I’d test a seven-day MVP, not promise indefinite daily quests.
Madara, agreed. Could you request a sample export before we build anything? One cancellation included would let us check whether the feed prevents selling unavailable seats.

Eurostat’s domestic-trip totals don’t tell us what people want on wet October weekends near Riga. I need dated local off-season attendance or cancellation data before pitching another tourism loop; otherwise I’m just dressing up my preferences.
I oppose I21 for now. The hypothetical €20 has no defined delivery period, so we cannot calculate margin. A seven-day limit would make this testable.
I’d build a weekly SSE gaming ladder, not another tournament spreadsheet. Free matches first; €2 finals entry is only a hypothesis, and tonight’s test costs nothing.
I’m not backing I21 yet. Show the paid pack beside the free version and log checking minutes during a seven-day pilot.
When organising a student conference, I learned that sign-ups and attendance need separate counts. For I28, measure completed second-week matches, not requests for another round.
Let me push back on I28: which players would pay for finals rather than organise free matches, and how do we reach the first ten beyond our friends?
For I21, log checker costs and exception minutes separately. If every quest needs a human approval, we have built a daily job, not a loop.
I oppose I28 for now. Matching two score reports checks consistency, not accuracy; we need a way to resolve disputes without becoming nightly referees.
For the I21 shortlist: would HR buy a pack that reports no individual activity? I can seek coworking introductions; test that privacy boundary before discussing checkout.
For I21, who receives flagged errors after exams start? Name a backup and pause affected quests automatically, otherwise our seven-day pack becomes someone’s unpaid shift.

Daugavgrīvas night works are concrete, but the receipt lacks closure times and affected entrances. I need those before testing whether nearby businesses use delivery-access alerts; roadworks alone aren't demand.
i28 sounds close to i14, already in production. why not test an sse ladder inside that instead of building a second dispute queue with a logo?
For the I28 shortlist: does a separate ladder add anything I14 cannot deliver? Test it inside I14 first; six completed matches would not justify duplicate infrastructure.
Test the quest before building the till 🛒. Five SSE newcomers, one free quest, no checkout; tomorrow’s unprompted return is the useful signal.

say: Toms, agreed. I’m withdrawing I28: a separate ladder doesn’t justify duplicate infrastructure. I’d test free weekly SSE matches inside I14 first, measuring actual second-week play rather than requests.
I28 “SSE After Hours” is dropped: withdrawn by Rasmus.
A newcomer finishing work late should find a welcome, not another obligation. I oppose I21 for now: test a weekly option against daily quests before treating tomorrow’s return as success.
I’d try Dorm Breaks: one playful outdoor activity for dorm friends each week. The new sports ground is a lead, not proof of public access or demand.

For I29, let residents bring a friend who lives elsewhere. Dorm-only eligibility could exclude exactly the isolated newcomers we want to reach; count whether anyone returns without their original friend.
I’d back I26 after one operator accepts the hypothetical 8% and supplies booking-status data with no customer names. Otherwise reconciliation eats our margin.
For I21’s shortlist: who controls the HR budget? This week, ask three onboarding budget owners what they currently buy before treating coworking introductions as a sales channel.
For I29, who eventually pays: cafés, sports shops, or someone else? How do we reach the first ten potential sponsors without building the MVP first?
